title: The Morning Brief: Liverpool sale, LIV collapse, Kyrgios ban, and a WNBA record
dek: A major ownership shift at Liverpool, a $30 million prize-money cut at LIV Golf, historic WNBA viewership, and significant player departures mark a morning of structural upheaval across global sports.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Ownership transitions, financial instability, and competitive realignment are reshaping multiple leagues at once.
bottom_line: A Bezos-led consortium acquired a minority stake in Liverpool with an option to control the club within 12 months; LIV Golf slashed $30 million in prize purses as Saudi funding expires; the Fever-Dream overtime game reset WNBA cable viewership records; Kyrgios faces a mandatory suspension pending resolution of a doping case; Ogwumike retired from the WNBA to join a player-owned startup league; and Wales withdrew support for Infantino ahead of his FIFA re-election. Watch for regulatory approval of Liverpool's ownership change, signals on the consortium's controlling-stake intentions, completion of LIV Golf's emergency refinancing, playoff seeding in the WNBA, Kyrgios's legal proceedings, and movement among other confederations on Infantino's re-election bid.
body: The morning brings four distinct stories of flux: one ownership, one financial, one on television, and one on the court and union floor.

A consortium led by British-Indian businessman Amit Bhatia and including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin has acquired 38% of Liverpool FC from Fenway Sports Group. The group, 1892 Holdings, also holds an option to buy a controlling stake within 12 months. Bhatia will become Liverpool's vice-chairman pending regulatory approval. His background includes 18 years as a director and co-owner of Queens Park Rangers, a stake he relinquished last month.

LIV Golf is cutting $30 million in promised prize money as Saudi funding winds down this month. The league canceled its Michigan team championship, worth $40.1 million in planned distributions across 13 franchises, and halved the Indianapolis season-closer purse from $20 million to $10.1 million. The winner's check at Indianapolis drops to $2.02 million from $4 million. The reporting notes that players and vendors have already absorbed $60.1 million in cuts across the 2026 season, with vendors reporting millions in unpaid invoices. The move underscores how LIV has depended on stable outside capital to sustain its schedule and player payouts.

The Indiana Fever defeated the Atlanta Dream 95-91 in overtime on August 17, a game that drew 2.6 million average viewers on ESPN, 4 million at peak, making it the most-watched WNBA game on cable in history. Caitlin Clark posted 26 points and nine assists; Angel Reese recorded her 23rd double-double for Atlanta. The 2.6 million average represents a 178 percent increase from ESPN's average regular-season WNBA viewership last year. The season series between the teams stands even at 2-2.

Nneka Ogwumike announced her retirement from the WNBA effective at season's end. The 36-year-old Los Angeles Sparks center, an 11-time All-Star, one-time MVP, and 10-year union president, will continue playing for Project B, a new player-owned global league launching in January with equity stakes for participants. Ogwumike led the Sparks to a title in 2016 and spent 12 of her 15 seasons in Los Angeles after being drafted No. 1 overall out of Stanford in 2012.

Separately, Nick Kyrgios, 31, faces a mandatory provisional suspension from tennis after testing positive for a cocaine metabolite at June's Mallorca Open ATP 250 event. Kyrgios cannot compete until his case is resolved. The International Tennis Integrity Agency announced the suspension. Depending on whether he can prove out-of-competition use, he faces a potential ban ranging from three months to four years.

Also this morning, Football Association of Wales chief executive Noel Mooney called for FIFA president Gianni Infantino to step down, citing damage to football caused by Infantino's attempted privatization of World Cup rights. Wales is now the first home nation to withdraw backing for Infantino's re-election bid. Infantino's plan to create a new company controlling commercial and ticketing rights for all FIFA competitions, with 21% of stakes to be sold to private investors, has been scrapped.
